extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, translators, and informed readers of Renaissance/French literature (especially Rabelais)
extracted.subtask_description: Literary-critical guidance and evaluative standards for reading, editing, translating, and judging the works of Rabelais (style, morality, sources, textual editing, and translation practice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use author's works as primary biographical source
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘his own work is the best and richest mine in which to search for the details of his life.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Biographical facts about Rabelais should be sought mainly within his writings rather than unreliable external anecdotes; his work provides the most trustworthy material for reconstructing his life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextualize coarse language historically
rubrics_metrics.description: Rabelais spoke 'as those of his time used to speak' and used popular contemporary language to be understood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge coarse or outspoken passages with attention to the literary and social atmosphere of the 16th century (Ancients, Fabliaux, Italian comic theatre, etc.) rather than by later standards alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid equating coarseness with moral corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Although often coarse, Rabelais 'has, after all, nothing unwholesome about it' and cannot be accused of inciting vice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether bawdy or coarse elements actually promote misconduct; the critic should ask whether the text tempts readers 'to stray from duty' or 'inspires feelings that breed misconduct and vice.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Studied coarseness can lower literary value
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'great reproach' is not mere lack of reserve but his 'occasional studied coarseness, which is enough to spoil his whole work, and which lowers its value.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish genuine comic or historical idiom from gratuitous coarseness; deliberate vulgarity that detracts from the work's merits is a valid critical fault.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not expurgate or 'modernize' the text
rubrics_metrics.description: Those 'who have brought out expurgated editions of him, or who have thought to improve him by trying to rewrite him in modern French, have been fools for their pains.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expurgation or rewriting to modernize Rabelais is condemned: editors/translators should preserve original force and character rather than attempt 'improving' it by censorship or modernization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dedications and privileges as evidence of contemporary reception
rubrics_metrics.description: His dedications and royal/papal privileges (e.g., Francis I. 1545; Henry II. 1550; Apostolic Pastorals) show acceptance by high personages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contemporary endorsements, dedications, and privileges are significant indicators of how Rabelais' work was received and should inform assessments of his standing in his own time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation requires more than ordinary familiarity with French
rubrics_metrics.description: There are 'few translations of Rabelais... the task is no light one, and demands more than a familiarity with ordinary French.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translators must command historical idioms, dialects, coined words, classical allusions, and the comic register; inadequate linguistic or cultural competence will fail to convey the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of censorship contexts when translating/publishing
rubrics_metrics.description: Spanish translation absent perhaps because 'The Inquisition would have been a far more serious opponent than the Paris’ Sorbonne.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider religious and political censorship environments that can affect what translations are possible or how they are shaped; choice of language/community matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good translation: fidelity to sense, vivacity, and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Urquhart 'renders the sense with a force and a vivacity full of warmth and brilliancy' and 'reproduces the very accent of the original, besides possessing a very remarkable character of its own.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A superior translation balances fidelity to meaning with recovery of the original’s vivacity, tone, and rhetorical force; literal adherence is less important than conveying spirit and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid undue liberties or embellishments in translation
rubrics_metrics.description: Fischart's work is 'not a translation, but a recast... full of alterations and of exaggerations' and added attacks and coarse expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not add material, polemical aims, or enlarged coarseness beyond the original; recasting that radically alters purpose or register is criticized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translations may be valuable in their own right if they create distinct works
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who modify others' ideas 'may be superior... but then the new works must be altogether different, must exist by themselves.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a translator/adapter substantially re-creates the text, it should be judged as an independent creative work rather than as a faithful translation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rabelais' vocabulary: mix popular speech, classical tongues, and neologisms
rubrics_metrics.description: He had 'something like three languages'—popular speech, Latin/Greek models, and fabricated words; his vocabulary is of astonishing variety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics and translators should attend to the multilingual blend, archaisms, and coinages; these are deliberate stylistic resources rather than mere incoherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neologisms and coinages as comic/artistic device (but can be excessive)
rubrics_metrics.description: He 'fabricated words... sometimes audaciously and with needless frequency' and 'coined an enormous number of interminable words' à la Aristophanes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize coinage as an important comic device; nonetheless, excessive or needless neologizing can be a stylistic fault to note.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority on textual variants: do not amalgamate differing readings
rubrics_metrics.description: A good edition 'would make no attempt at amalgamating' variants 'but it should note them all, and show them all, not combined, but simply as variations.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should present variant readings transparently (apparatus or notes), avoid fabricating a synthetic text by conflating contradictory variants, and document suppressions/additions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial method should consider authorial revision practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Rabelais' revisions often consist of insertions that preserve the former clause 'in its integrity along with the additional one' rather than wholesale rewriting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual scholarship should account for the author's incremental revision style (small insertions and additions) when reconstructing textual histories or establishing editions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two valid editorial approaches: latest text with variants or first text with later modifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Since Jannet's edition gave 'Rabelais’ latest text... accompanied by all the earlier variations,' it is also 'possible to reverse the method' and take his first text as basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both presenting the final revised text with variants and presenting the earliest text with later modifications are instructive editorial approaches; choose method according to scholarly aim and be explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require documentary evidence before asserting folkloric antecedents
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that Gargantua is of Celtic origin are unjustified without 'positive traces'—there is no written passage proving the name before Rabelais.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid speculative origins; require positive documentary or textual traces before asserting lineage of characters or motifs from earlier folk traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trace classical and contemporary sources carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Rabelais owed much to Aristophanes, Lucian, Pliny, Poggio's Facetiae, and other known works; some borrowings are explicit, others are subtle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars should trace influences across classical and contemporary sources, recognizing both overt quotations and subtle adaptation, including the use of fictitious authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess genre-specific competency (prose vs verse vs letters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rabelais 'had no gift of poetic form... his letters are bombastic and thin... he is only a literary artist when he wishes to be such; and in his romance he changes the style completely.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate different genres separately: excellence in novelistic prose does not imply skill in verse or epistolary writing; criticism should be sensitive to genre-specific strengths/weaknesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware localist appropriations without evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Provincials 'have been too eager to appropriate him, to make of him a local author' and dialect-patriots 'have fallen out among themselves.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid attributing Rabelais' linguistic features or origin too readily to a single local dialect without careful linguistic and documentary support.
